get.description: Carries `has_player_profile`, the fourth branch of onboarding's entry gate. It is read from the profile's event stream rather than from a projection, so a player who has just committed their profile is never sent back into the social steps by a read model that has not caught up.

post.summary: Authenticate and obtain an access/refresh token pair
Start an assessment and receive its opening question
post.description:
Idempotent per player and sport. Starting a sport that already has an unfinished run returns **that** run and its outstanding question with a 200, rather than opening a second one — so a double-tapped confirm, or a retry after a lost response, costs nothing. A sport whose previous run was abandoned still starts a new run, with a 201.

Both outcomes carry the same body, so a client that only routes on the step needs no branch; the status code is there for one that wants to tell the two apart.

**A sport this player is already rated at is refused with a 409** (`sport_already_rated`). A rating stream is keyed by player and sport and initialisation is its only transition, so a second completed run for one sport cannot be stored — and refusing at the start is the only point at which refusing costs the player nothing rather than a whole questionnaire. The picker offers unrated sports, so no shipped flow reaches this.

201.description: A new assessment was started; its opening question is returned.

200.description: An assessment for this sport was already in progress; its outstanding question is returned and nothing was created.

409.description: `sport_already_rated` — this player already holds a Skill rating for this sport, so no assessment is started.

get.summary: Resume: one sport's in-progress assessment, or every sport's
get.description:
One question — *which of this player's runs are unfinished* — asked two ways.

**With `sport`,** the answer is that sport's outstanding run as an `AssessmentStepResponse`, carrying its outstanding question, or a 204 when there is none. This is the resume read, unchanged.

**Without `sport`,** the answer is an `InProgressAssessmentsResponse`: every unfinished run this player holds, at most one per sport, ordered by the sport registry, and an empty list — with a 200, never a 204 or a 404 — when there are none. Each entry carries the assessment id and its sport, which is what a router needs; it carries no question, because the caller re-reads the run it routes to and the empty answer is the common one.

Which shape comes back is decided by the parameter, so a caller that always omits `sport` always sees the collection.

schema.title: Response Find In Progress Api V1 Assessments In Progress Get

204.description: No assessment in progress for that sport. Only ever returned when `sport` is supplied.

get.summary: Fetch an assessment's current state — its question or its result

post.summary: Finish a stopped assessment: create its Skill rating
post.description:
**The irreversible one.** The questionnaire *stopping* and the assessment *completing* are two moments: answering the question that stops the run creates nothing and leaves every answer revisable, and this request is what turns those answers into a Skill rating. So a client can show the whole set of answers back to the player, still changeable, before anything is committed.

Callable only on a **stopped** run — one whose step carries neither a `question` nor a `result` while `status` is still `in_progress`. A run with a question outstanding, and one that was abandoned, are both refused with `assessment_not_stopped`.

The finished step comes back inline, `result` and all, because the player is shown their rating on the very next screen. **Calling it twice is safe**: the second call records nothing and returns the same result, so a double-tapped submit produces one rating rather than a conflict the client has to translate.

Once this has been called the run's answers are settled: a change is refused with `answer_not_revisable`.

409.description: `assessment_not_stopped` — the questionnaire has not finished asking, or the run was abandoned. Refetch the current step and render it.

post.summary: Abandon an in-progress assessment, freeing the sport to start again
Answer the outstanding question, or change an answer already given
post.description:
**One request, decided by what the run has already answered.**

- A `question_id` the run has *not* answered must be the outstanding one: this is an ordinary answer, and the next question comes back — or **no question at all**, which is the questionnaire stopping.
- A `question_id` the run *has* answered with a **different** `option_id` is a **revision**. The answers given after it are discarded, because each was pitched at a difficulty chosen from the estimate as it then stood, and the response is whatever the questionnaire asks next given the shortened set of answers. That may be a question, and it may be the stop — changing the opening answer to *I have never played* ends the questioning there.
- A `question_id` the run has answered with the **same** `option_id` records nothing and returns the current step. So a retry after a lost response is free, and so is changing your mind and changing it back.

**`question` and `result` both null, with `status` still `in_progress`, is the stop.** No further question would meaningfully tighten the estimate, and nothing has been rated: the run waits, with every answer still revisable, until `POST /completion` is called. Answering never creates a Skill rating, so a client need not — and cannot — predict which question is the last one.

The `transcript` on every response is the answers as they now stand; after a revision it is **shorter**, and a client showing the run's progress should read it rather than remember what it last drew.

**Answers are revisable for as long as the run is, and no longer.** Once the run has produced a Skill rating, a change is refused with `answer_not_revisable` — a code of its own, because the recovery is to show the rating rather than to re-render a question.

400.description: `invalid_answer_option` — the chosen option is not one that question offers.

409.description: `question_not_outstanding` — the question is neither the one awaiting a response nor one this run has answered; refetch the current step and re-render it. `answer_not_revisable` — this run's Skill rating already exists, so its answers are settled; show the rating instead.

get.summary: The Skill ratings this player holds, one per rated sport
The Social tag vocabulary and how many to pick, and the Search radius bounds
get.description:
Read-only, unauthenticated, no request body. Tag **ids** and their grouping cross the wire; the label a player reads is the client's own copy.

A tag id is permanent — it is persisted on profiles, so retiring a tag means dropping it from this response while continuing to honour it on the profiles that hold it. Ids are never reused and never renamed.

Both the group order and the tag order within a group are part of the contract: the picker renders what it is given rather than sorting.

`social_tag_selection` carries how many tags a profile must hold — both ends included. The profile commit re-validates against the same numbers, so a picker that reads them here cannot disagree with it.

post.summary: Commit every answer from onboarding's second part
post.description:
Idempotent per `Idempotency-Key`. The same key twice creates one profile and returns the same body — the second call answers 200 and records nothing.

**Every rule the picker enforced is re-validated here.** The tag vocabulary, the tag floor and ceiling and the radius bounds are all served by `GET /player-profile/options` so a client can build controls that cannot produce an illegal value — and a disabled button is not a validation. Photo ids are checked to exist *and* to belong to the caller.

**An empty availability grid is accepted.** Blank means no preference; it is never read as *leave me out*, and it excludes the player from nothing.

**The proposals opt-in has no default.** Send the player's actual answer; `null` is refused rather than treated as a no. The answer is recorded with the moment, the copy version shown and the surface, because consent is evidenced rather than asserted.

parameters.name: Idempotency-Key

schema.description: What the client calls this commit. Sending the same key again returns the profile the first call created, with a 200 — one profile, one consent answer, whatever a flaky connection does to the response.
schema.title: Idempotency-Key

parameters.description: What the client calls this commit. Sending the same key again returns the profile the first call created, with a 200 — one profile, one consent answer, whatever a flaky connection does to the response.

200.description: This idempotency key has already been committed; the profile the first call created is returned and nothing was recorded.

400.description:
`unknown_social_tag` — an id this platform does not serve; re-read `GET /player-profile/options`.

`social_tag_selection_out_of_bounds` — too few or too many tags for the served floor and ceiling.

`duplicate_social_tag` — the same tag id arrived twice.

`search_radius_out_of_bounds` — outside the served range, or off its step.

`proposals_opt_in_not_answered` — the answer was `null`. Ask the question; do not send `false` on the player's behalf.

`too_many_photos` / `duplicate_photo` — the photo list is not one a profile may hold.

404.description: `photo_not_found` — a photo id that does not exist, or belongs to another player. The two answer the same way deliberately.

409.description:
`player_profile_already_exists` — this player has a profile and this is a **different** idempotency key, so it is a second commit rather than a retry of the first.

`concurrent_modification` — two commits for this player raced and this one lost. Retry: the retry replays the winner.

post.description:
One photo per request. The body is the raw image and `Content-Type` names its format; JPEG, PNG and HEIC/HEIF are accepted.

**What is stored is not what was sent.** Every image is decoded and re-encoded to JPEG with its long edge capped, which is how EXIF — and with it the GPS coordinates a phone writes into a photo — is removed reliably rather than best-effort.

The returned id is what a profile commit carries; a photo becomes part of a profile only when a commit names it. Uploaded photos that are never committed are intended to be swept, and that sweep is not running yet.

get.summary: A signed URL for one of your photos
get.description:
Returns a short-lived signed URL rather than the bytes: the store serves the image directly, so a photo never crosses this API twice.

A photo id that does not exist and one belonging to another player both answer `photo_not_found`, deliberately — the alternative is an endpoint that confirms whether a stranger's id is real.

status.title: Status
status.description:
`in_progress`, `completed` or `abandoned` — and the field that says which of two things *neither a question nor a result* means.

- `in_progress` **with** a `question`: the questionnaire, awaiting that answer.
- `in_progress` with **neither**: the questionnaire has **stopped**. No remaining question would meaningfully tighten the estimate, and nothing has been rated — every answer is still revisable, and `POST /assessments/{assessment_id}/completion` is what creates the Skill rating.
- `completed`: the `result` is here and the answers are settled.
- `abandoned`: neither, and the run ended without a rating.

questions_asked.title: Questions Asked
questions_asked.description: How many of this run's questions have been answered. The outstanding `question` is **not** counted — it has been put to the player but not answered — so a question counter reads this plus one, and a fresh run reports 0. Replayed from the transcript on every read, which is what lets a resumed run report the position it is really at rather than restarting at 1. Once the run is over this is the same number `result.questions_asked` carries.

transcript.title: Transcript
transcript.description: Every answer given in this run so far, in the order they were given, each with the question it answered **as that question was asked** — so an answered question can be rendered from the response alone, by a client that was never shown it. Empty, never absent, on a run with no answers yet: a fresh run and a run whose answers are being withheld are not two readings of one payload. Grows by one entry per answer and is replayed from the stream on every read, so it survives a reinstall and a second device with nothing cached locally. Length is `questions_asked`; the outstanding `question` is not in it, because it has not been answered.

AssessmentStepResponse.title: AssessmentStepResponse
AssessmentStepResponse.description:
The server-driven step: at most one of `question` / `result` is set, and
`transcript` is everything already answered behind it. Neither means the run
is not asking and has not been rated — see `status`.

day.title: Day
day.description: ISO weekday — 1 is Monday, 7 is Sunday. The grid is Monday-first.

AvailabilitySlotResource.title: AvailabilitySlotResource
AvailabilitySlotResource.description:
One ticked cell of the availability grid.

Two named fields rather than the single joined code the event stream stores.
The stream's code is a *storage* encoding chosen so a replay folds strings;
this is a contract a client renders a grid from, and a client that had to
split ``"3:EVENING"`` would be parsing our persistence format.

social_tag_ids.title: Social Tag Ids
social_tag_ids.description: The tag ids this player picked, as served by `GET /player-profile/options`. The count is re-checked against the served floor and ceiling, and an id this platform does not serve is refused with `unknown_social_tag`.

photo_ids.title: Photo Ids
photo_ids.description: Ids returned by `POST /photos`, in the order the player arranged them — the first is the one a player card shows. At most 3; an empty list is valid. Every id is checked to exist and to belong to this player.

availability.title: Availability
availability.description: The cells of the week this player ticked. **An empty list is a valid answer** and means no preference — it is never read as unavailable. Repeated cells are collapsed.

search_radius_km.title: Search Radius Km
search_radius_km.description: Whole kilometres, re-checked against the range and step served by `GET /player-profile/options`.

CommitPlayerProfileRequest.title: CommitPlayerProfileRequest
CommitPlayerProfileRequest.description:
Every answer from onboarding's second part, in one body.

Photos and availability default to empty because both are legitimately
blank: a player may hold no photos, and **a blank week means "no preference"
and never "leave me out"**. Nothing else has a default — a location, a
radius, a tag selection and an answer to the proposals question are all
things this request must actually carry.

ConfidenceReasonResponse.title: ConfidenceReasonResponse
ConfidenceReasonResponse.description: Why confidence landed where it did: a stable key and the sentence shown.

ConsentSurface.title: ConsentSurface
ConsentSurface.description:
Where a player was standing when they answered.

Two values, and both are reachable. ``ONBOARDING`` is the only one the commit
can record — the commit *is* the end of onboarding's second part. The profile
screen edits the same value later (``docs/adr/0089``), which is what
``PROFILE`` is for; the aggregate transition it uses exists, and the endpoint
that drives it does not yet.

DayPart.title: DayPart
DayPart.description:
The three parts of a day a player may tick.

Closed, and deliberately coarse. The product asks *when do you usually play*,
and an answer finer than this would be a schedule — which is the thing a
preference is explicitly not.

Declared in rendering order, so ``tuple(DayPart)`` is the order a grid is
laid out in and no caller sorts.

ErrorResponse.description: The body of every error response, on both API surfaces.

code.description: Stable, machine-readable identifier for this exact failure. The only half of the envelope a client may branch on.
code.title: Code

message.description: Human-readable diagnostic. Never the copy shown to a user — that is the client's, chosen from the code.
message.title: Message

trace_id.description: This request's identifier, also returned on the X-Request-ID header. Ties a client-side failure to a server log without logging a payload.
trace_id.title: Trace Id

details.description: Structured context for this code, when the code defines any.
details.title: Details

ErrorResponse.title: ErrorResponse

FactorResponse.title: FactorResponse
FactorResponse.description:
One evidence category's row: what it says, and which way it pulled.

``direction`` is one of ``up`` / ``down`` / ``neutral``, computed by the
engine from that category's own evidence against the final estimate. The
client never derives it — a client-side arrow is a second opinion about the
arithmetic, and two clients would eventually hold two of them.

InProgressAssessmentResponse.title: InProgressAssessmentResponse
InProgressAssessmentResponse.description:
One unfinished run: which assessment, and which sport it is for.

Carries no question, no result and no progress. A caller reading this is
deciding *where to send the player*; it re-reads the run it routes to, and
that read is the one that reproduces the outstanding question.

InProgressAssessmentsResponse.title: InProgressAssessmentsResponse
InProgressAssessmentsResponse.description:
Every unfinished run this player holds — empty when they hold none.

Empty is the ordinary answer for a new account and for a player who has
finished everything they started, so it is a 200 with an empty list rather
than a 404 or the singular form's 204.

Ordered by the sport registry, so a caller that wants one run can take the
first entry.

LocationAreaResource.title: LocationAreaResource
LocationAreaResource.description:
Where a player plays.

**What is sent and what is kept are not the same number.** A client sends the
fix its device gave it; the platform rounds to roughly a kilometre before
anything is recorded, and it is the rounded pair that comes back here. The
precise fix is never stored and never shareable
(``../../../../CONTEXT.md`` — *Location area*).

photo_id.title: Photo Id
photo_id.description: Permanent id — what the profile commit carries

url.title: Url
url.description: Short-lived signed URL that reads this photo. Not a stable address: it is signed for one player, for one window, and there is no public bucket behind it.

expires_at.title: Expires At
expires_at.description: When the URL stops working. Ask for the photo again to get another; there is no way to extend one.

PhotoResponse.title: PhotoResponse
PhotoResponse.description:
One photo: the id a profile commit will carry, and a URL that reads it.

The same shape from the upload and from the read, so a client renders a tile
it has just filled and a tile it is restoring with one code path.

**The URL is not an identifier and must not be stored as one.** It carries a
signature and stops working at ``expires_at``; the id is what is permanent.

PlayerProfileOptionsResponse.title: PlayerProfileOptionsResponse
PlayerProfileOptionsResponse.description:
Everything a client needs to *render* the profile steps, in one round trip.

A handful of facts rather than one endpoint each, because they are the same
kind of thing — closed, read-only, and needed by the same part of onboarding
at the same moment.

**Fields are only ever added.** A shipped mobile app parses this document for
months after it stops being built, so a new field goes on the end and the
ones already here keep their names and their types.

PlayerProfileResponse.title: PlayerProfileResponse
PlayerProfileResponse.description:
A player's profile as it now stands.

The same body whether the commit created the profile or replayed an earlier
one, so a client that only wants its profile needs no branch on the status.

**Fields are only ever added.** A shipped mobile app parses this document for
months after it stops being built.

accepted.title: Accepted
accepted.description: The player's answer. `null` means the question was not answered, which is refused — it is never read as `false`.

copy_version.title: Copy Version
copy_version.description: Identifier of the exact copy the player was shown. Not the copy itself — the words are the client's and are never stored here.

ProposalsOptInRequest.title: ProposalsOptInRequest
ProposalsOptInRequest.description:
The answer to the proposals question, and the words it was given against.

``accepted`` is **nullable and required**, which is the shape of a question
that has no default. Null means *not answered* and is refused by the commit
with ``proposals_opt_in_not_answered``; it is not a quiet ``false``, because
a recorded refusal and an unanswered question are different facts and only
one of them is consent (``../../../../CONTEXT.md`` — *Skipping is not
consent*).

``copy_version`` identifies the exact wording the player was shown. It is
required because consent gathered against one sentence is not consent to a
different one, and a consent record that cannot name its words cannot
evidence anything.

copy_version.title: Copy Version
copy_version.description: The copy this answer was given against

ProposalsOptInResponse.title: ProposalsOptInResponse
ProposalsOptInResponse.description:
The standing answer, and the evidence recorded with it.

This is the *current* answer. The **history** — every answer this player ever
gave, against which words and on which surface — is the stream, and nothing
serves it yet because nothing has asked for it.

QuestionResponse.title: QuestionResponse
QuestionResponse.description: A question in reading order: category, situation, question, answers.

RatingResponse.title: RatingResponse
RatingResponse.description:
One sport's Skill rating.

``mu`` and ``sigma`` are the Level and the Uncertainty — the same spelling
``ResultResponse`` already puts on the wire for the same two numbers, so a
client never has to learn that the rating it was just shown and the rating it
later reads back are described in two vocabularies.

RatingsResponse.title: RatingsResponse
RatingsResponse.description: Every sport this player is rated at — empty when they are rated at none.

confidence_ceiling.title: Confidence Ceiling
confidence_ceiling.description: The highest `confidence` this engine version can reach, as a whole percent — a questionnaire has an irreducible limit, so a rating at this value was held by the ceiling and one below it by its own evidence. Absent only for a rating replayed from an engine version that has since been retired, which is the same case that carries no `confidence_reason`: such a rating keeps its numbers and loses its explanation. Do not hold a local copy of this number — it is version-scoped and may be retuned without a client release.

minimum_km.title: Minimum Km
minimum_km.description: Smallest radius a player may hold

maximum_km.title: Maximum Km
maximum_km.description: Largest radius a player may hold

SearchRadiusBoundsResource.title: SearchRadiusBoundsResource
SearchRadiusBoundsResource.description:
The range a Search radius may take, in whole kilometres.

The unit is in every field name on purpose: a bare ``minimum`` is one
refactor away from being read as metres.

SocialTag.title: SocialTag
SocialTag.description: The closed set of tag ids. An id here is permanent.

SocialTagGroup.title: SocialTagGroup
SocialTagGroup.description: The three groups, which are about the game and nothing else.

SocialTagGroupResource.title: SocialTagGroupResource
SocialTagGroupResource.description: One of the three groups, with its tags in the order they are rendered.

SocialTagResource.title: SocialTagResource
SocialTagResource.description:
One tag, as an id and nothing else — for now.

An object rather than a bare string deliberately: retiring a tag is
anticipated (an id is honoured forever and hidden from the picker), and a
tag that carries a field one day is an addition here, where an array of
strings would have to change element type — which breaks a shipped client.

minimum_tags.title: Minimum Tags
minimum_tags.description: Fewest tags a player may hold — the picker's floor

maximum_tags.title: Maximum Tags
maximum_tags.description: Most tags a player may hold — the picker's ceiling

SocialTagSelectionBoundsResource.title: SocialTagSelectionBoundsResource
SocialTagSelectionBoundsResource.description:
How many Social tags a selection must hold to be one.

The unit is in both field names for the reason it is on the radius bounds:
a bare ``minimum`` beside a list of eighteen tags reads as a count of
something, and which something is exactly what a client would guess wrong.

Sport.title: Sport
Sport.description: The four sports Raketa rates, as a closed enum.

players.title: Players
players.description: Number of players the sport is played for

SportResource.title: SportResource
SportResource.description: One sport as served: how many play it and the durations it is sold in.

TranscriptEntryResponse.title: TranscriptEntryResponse
TranscriptEntryResponse.description: One answered question: the question as it was asked, and what was chosen.

UncertaintyFactorResponse.title: UncertaintyFactorResponse
UncertaintyFactorResponse.description: Something that widened the range instead of moving the estimate.

has_player_profile.title: Has Player Profile
has_player_profile.description: Whether this player has committed a Player profile — the fourth branch of the entry gate. Read from the profile's own event stream rather than from a projection, so it is correct immediately after the commit that creates one. False on a response that is not about the authenticated player, such as the one registration returns.

UserResponse.title: UserResponse
UserResponse.description:
The account, plus the one fact about it onboarding's entry gate needs.

``has_player_profile`` is not a property of a ``User`` and the domain layer
has no idea it exists — it is answered by the Player profile context and
joined here, on the response, because the gate reads it on every cold launch
and a second round trip for one boolean would be a second thing to fail
(``docs/adr/0090``).

**It is not an "onboarded" flag.** The rating context's invariant against one
stands: whether a player has been through onboarding *for a sport* is asked
by asking whether a rating exists for that sport, and this field cannot
answer it. This asks a genuinely per-player question, because a profile is
one per player and has no sport dimension at all.
